77.history: The walled temple city in the north-east is the seat of the house of disputation. Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais who had walked the carters' roads for forty years, raised Taigh na Deasbaid here in LE 314 and had the schools' old question, Carson an làmh seo?, cut into its lintel before the roof was on; a question once put was argued a full year before any answer came from the master's chair. Pupils walked three days from Caol bheag to sit its benches. In LE 324 Coinneach asked there whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and each of the seven houses forbade the question at its own table. Ailean mac Dhùghaill's tables of the three old ruins were judged here, and in the thirteenth century Raghnall mac Chaluim set out here the table of years that showed the heads of the houses living longer than their tenants; the table was forbidden and the house shut. It was opened and shut more than once, and last reopened in LE 1,759 on condition that the question of longer lives never be raised; its schools turned instead to whether the custody-book's handful answered to what the coal gave out.
77.known_for: the house of disputation, and the questions it was forbidden

76.history: The small walled river town of the north-east found its fortune in LE 350, when a farmer digging a ditch above it struck warm water that tasted of salt. Pans were laid out on the flats within the season, and the salt went inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn, whose keeper Iain mac Ùisdein took a handful from every load for his toll and filled an iron-bound salt-box faster than any box on that road. Ros fhionn salted the fish of the mining shires, and at the height of its fair in LE 959 the reeve lost his count past four thousand people on the flats. The salt-masters rebuilt the bridge's arches at their own cost in the twelfth century after a carter's mule went into the river through the road bed. Then a shifting bar silted the Abhainn bheag, the barges could no longer reach the quays, and the salt went by sea through Caol gharbh; the market-court stayed on its headland with its bench of old oak, the bridge's last keeper died with no one to take the toll, and the channel was withied from the bar to open water.
76.known_for: its salt, its bridge and its market-court

443.history: The fishing village on the rough strait of the north-east became the salt port of the north-east in LE 1,169, when the Ros fhionn masters dug out and walled its harbour with their own money after their river silted. A laden barge out of the new harbour struck the reef in the narrows called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich in its first year and went down with half her salt, both crewmen swimming ashore; the harbour-masters set the channel's first withy at the rock the next spring. The trade held for five and a half centuries, until the sea rose over the salt-pans in LE 1,734 and they failed, and the salt of the north-east came from the south instead.
443.known_for: the salt harbour, and the narrows

131.history: The weavers of the north-eastern town make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and in the fourth century of the count it became the common cloak of the north-east. In LE 361 the district took it as its cloth of mourning, worn plain through a household's season of loss as the whole island had once worn the white sorrow, and the white sorrow was kept in it in that country from then on.
131.known_for: the undyed rain-cloth worn for mourning

333.history: The village in the north-eastern hills is where Eilidh nic Iain, Eilidh Dhubh, taught at the well from LE 460, at thirty years old, the teaching her grandmother had taught her in secret: that the vein answers labour and not birth. She wrote it down in a hand her mother taught her, and pupils copied her tracts for households too far to hear her. When the vein-house burned some hundred of them in its yard in LE 484 she walked there to see it done and said nothing. One hide in her mother's hand stayed whole in a hollow beam of her house. She died here in LE 505, teaching within the hour of her death, and was buried behind her own house; Coinneach Odhar read the tracts at her grave from the copy he had carried thirty years.

246.history: The mill town on the hill road of the east had a widow's loft by the seventeenth century of the count. Beathag nic Thòmais, whose husband had owned its mill, began in LE 1,659 to buy old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them, and in her loft a crown clerk found the only surviving copy of a custodians' ruling the vein-house had lost to fire. In LE 1,674 Anna nic Coinnich began to make paper from rags at the town's ford, the first on Dia-thìr; Beathag carried it sixty miles to the vein-house herself, and the custody-book was copied onto it for the first time. Among her papers she found three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls that did not agree, copied all three fair, and chose none. She left the loft to the town when she died in LE 1,699, on condition that nothing in it be burned, and the town kept the condition; its unpaid keeper told a crown reeve that fifty years of neither office asking for the papers back was itself an answer.
246.known_for: the paper mill and the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais

175.history: The deep ford on the northern river could be crossed safely only on horseback and by one path, and in LE 1,611 Raghnall Àthach and his kin, who knew that path, settled on the near bank and took a toll of every rider they led over. The ford-keepers' households grew into a town that held the one safe crossing of that country, and the family that owned the path came to be spoken of as lords of it before the age was out.

136.history: The citadel on the straight eastern road, raised by custodians of the road in the Holy Age, was granted a market for the east coast in LE 731, and its boundary stones were set the day the grant was read, with a young vein-house scribe, Eòghann mac Pheadair, standing witness for the seven houses. The fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns met the grain of the inland farms there, and the first stalls went up the same afternoon.
136.known_for: the market of the eastern road

411.history: The farming country of the far east caught the rain the eastern hills always had until three seasons ran dry from LE 1,479, and the crown's grain carts reached it by the mining road. Its reeves shared the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn and cut the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board was renewed each generation; the lots were never drawn again. When Queen Sìleas Òg stood at the well-head on her round and asked why, the reeve answered that no household wished to be the one to call the first sharing unfair, and she rode on without asking him to change it.

387.history: The walled town of the east by Seann Tarr held an autumn cattle fair that in LE 1,519 began to draw the drovers of Àth chiar and the eastern hills, who brought their beasts down to it rather than sell nearer home. It became yearly, and within a few years the greatest fair in the east.
387.known_for: the cattle fair of the east

119.history: The eastern harbour, a hundred miles from the west coast over the mountain country, kept the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night. Six pilots of the west walked to it in LE 11 and were sent to the old steersman Seumas Reultach, who taught them on the headland above the town the wheel of the sky and the steering star, Reul na Stiùire, and had his granddaughter cut part of it on a hide; he died on the cliff path in LE 14 and is buried among his own people. After the pilots went west nobody at Cuan ruadh sailed by night any longer. In the fifteenth century it built a second harbour arm to take the boats of Seann Tarr when that harbour broke, and throve on the fishing of both towns' waters for the rest of the age.
119.known_for: the star-steersmen, and its second harbour arm

34.history: The small citadel harbour of the east kept an ancestor shrine of the Old Spirits, and from LE 644 the crowds that came to it for the great feasts held a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey, beeswax for the shrine's lights and the wool of the hill farms. The market outgrew the feasts in time and was held whether the shrine had a feast or not.

276.history: The village among the wells of the eastern hill country keeps the naming rites of the old reciters. At a naming there in LE 525, for a steward's son of Tormod Bàn's household, the reciter Muireach mac Ailein of Clann na Ceiste said the line of the Mason over the child instead of the long line of the Stone Kings that royal namings there had called on for generations.

249.history: The old harbour of the east coast below Cuan ruadh was torn apart in LE 1,399 by the storm the coast called Gailleann Ghlas, which came in out of the east and left the village standing but its quay in pieces past any mending worth the cost. Its boats went to Cuan ruadh, which built a second harbour arm to take them. Seann Tarr kept its houses and its shrine, let its harbour go, and was entered in the charter-roll, in the roll's own dry word for such places, as a village again.
249.known_for: the harbour given up after Gailleann Ghlas
